A provider directory makes care look findable. What happens when someone tries to use it?

By Megan Quigley · A synthesis of published research

Follow the story ↓

From a coverage card to an appointment

01 Coverage02 Directory03 Calls04 Waits05 Access

01 / Coverage

Covered

Medicaid finances mental-health care. In managed care, state agencies contract with health plans to deliver covered benefits. This makes access a public-service question even when the people answering the phone work for a private practice.

Coverage, a listed clinician, an offered appointment, and a completed visit are different milestones. This story follows one of those transitions: from a directory listing to an appointment offer.

The focus is adult psychiatric prescribing care through Medicaid managed care. It is not an assessment of every mental-health service, every therapist, or every Medicaid program.

Medicaid.gov: managed-care delivery ↗Medicaid.gov: behavioral-health services ↗

02 / Directory

Listed

Researchers selected 80 psychiatric prescribing clinicians in each of four cities: New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Phoenix. The clinicians appeared in directories for each city’s highest-enrollment Medicaid managed-care plan and were listed as accepting new patients.

That made 320 offices to contact. The calls took place in 2023; the study was published in 2024. Researchers requested the earliest appointment and asked about an alternate clinician if the selected clinician was unavailable.

On a screen, 320 listings can look like 320 opportunities. The next step is to test what those opportunities mean.

JAMA: audit methods and results ↗

03 / Calls

Contacted

Appointments were available with the selected clinician at 57 offices. Another 30 offered an alternate clinician at the same practice. Together, 87 of 320 offices—27.2%—offered an appointment.

At the other 233 offices, the study did not obtain an appointment. That group should not be described as 233 fake clinicians. An unsuccessful attempt does not, by itself, establish fraud or explain everything about a practice.

Keep all three groups visible. The distinction matters: counting only the selected clinician would miss the alternatives that were offered. Counting every directory entry as accessible would miss the gap the calls revealed.

JAMA: four-city Medicaid appointment audit ↗

04 / Waits

Waiting

An appointment offer still leaves another question: when?

Among appointments with recorded wait times, city medians were 11 days in Phoenix, 23 in Chicago, 28 in New York City, and 64 in Los Angeles. Wait-time information was unavailable for 17 of the 87 offers without more extensive registration.

The calendar adds a dimension that the directory cannot show. An entry tells someone where to begin; the earliest available date tells them something different about whether help is within reach.

These medians describe observed offers, not the experience of everyone in those cities. Nor did the audit establish that an appointment was attended or that treatment helped. Those outcomes would require different evidence.

JAMA: wait times and missing observations (Figure 1) ↗

05 / Access

Accountable

A public service needs ways to check whether the route it gives people actually works.

A separate 2025 federal inspector general review examined selected Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed-care networks. It found that inactive listings could make networks appear larger than they were. Its Medicaid-specific recommendation was for CMS to work with states to improve directory accuracy.

That recommendation is a starting point for accountability, not evidence that access has already improved. Correct contact information is valuable; whether a person can obtain appropriate, timely care remains a further question.

For this story, the closing questions are practical: Can someone reach the office? Can the practice offer an appointment through the plan? How long is the wait? What happens when the first option is unavailable?

A directory can be the beginning of a public service. Its usefulness should be judged by where it leads.

What this story can tell us

This is an audit of adult psychiatric prescribing appointments in four cities, with calls in 2023. It is not a national rate, a study of every form of therapy, or a record of completed treatment. The study did not include a commercial-insurance comparison group.

Illustrations explain a process. They do not depict an interviewed person. Recommendations and editorial questions are labeled separately from measured results.
